# How to use this guide

Physical Pharmaceutics II links physical chemistry to real dosage forms: colloids, flow behaviour, suspensions and emulsions, powders, and drug stability. About half of the scoring answers need a diagram (rheogram, double layer, hysteresis loop, sedimentation plot, Arrhenius plot) and many need a short calculation. Study one unit a day: read the notes, redo every worked example with a calculator without looking, draw each diagram once from memory, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers.

The notes follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 2 also contains "Deformation of solids" (stress, strain, elastic modulus, Heckel equation), which the syllabus places under rheology.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays: attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers: attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High:** asked in most years; prepare the full answer with diagrams, equations and a worked numerical.
- **Medium:** asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low:** rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Colloids | Lyophilic vs lyophobic vs association colloids, optical and kinetic properties, electrical double layer and zeta potential, protective colloids and gold number, coacervation |
| 2 Rheology | Newton's law, types of non-Newtonian flow with rheograms, thixotropy and its uses, viscometers (Ostwald, falling sphere, cup-and-bob, cone-and-plate), Heckel equation |
| 3 Coarse dispersions | Flocculated vs deflocculated suspensions, Stokes's law, sedimentation volume and degree of flocculation, theories of emulsification, emulsion stability, HLB calculations |
| 4 Micromeritics | Methods of particle size analysis (microscopy, sieving, sedimentation), mean diameters, surface area methods, densities and porosity, flow properties |
| 5 Drug stability | Order of reaction with derivations, half-life and shelf life, determination of order, Arrhenius equation and accelerated stability testing, hydrolysis and oxidation prevention |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Start every answer with a one-line definition and the key equation; then explain each symbol with its unit.
2. For derivations (first order, second order, Stokes, Arrhenius), write the differential form, integrate, give the linear plot and the half-life. Examiners mark each step.
3. Numericals: write the formula, substitute with units, and box the answer with its unit (cP, day⁻¹, M⁻¹ min⁻¹, cm²/g, %). Method marks are given even if the arithmetic slips.
4. Draw the matching graph every time: rheograms of the four flow types, hysteresis loop, double layer with zeta potential, zeta potential vs electrolyte concentration (caking diagram), log-normal distribution, log k vs pH, log k vs 1/T.
5. Comparison tables score well: lyophilic vs lyophobic, flocculated vs deflocculated, macro- vs microemulsion, elastic vs plastic deformation, specific vs general catalysis.
6. End essays with 3–4 pharmaceutical applications (suspension design, thixotropic depot injections, micronisation for absorption, shelf-life prediction).
7. Practise these numerical types until they are automatic: Ostwald viscosity, Stokes settling rate, sedimentation volume and β, HLB of a blend and required HLB of an oil mix, mean diameters from a frequency table, specific surface, porosity and Carr's index, angle of repose, k, t½ and t90 for each order, and Arrhenius extrapolation.
8. Learn the standard values: t90 = 0.105/k, t½ = 0.693/k, water ≈ 1 cP at 20 °C, closest and open packing porosity 26% and 48%, w/o HLB 3–6 and o/w HLB 8–18, accelerated condition 40 °C/75% RH.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics with full diagrams and one worked numerical each: **types of colloids with zeta potential and protective action**, **non-Newtonian flow and thixotropy with viscometers**, **flocculated vs deflocculated suspensions with Stokes's law and sedimentation volume**, **particle size methods with derived properties of powders**, and **orders of reaction with Arrhenius-based accelerated stability testing**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**One-line contrasts examiners like**

| Pair | Difference |
| --- | --- |
| Lyophilic vs lyophobic | Solvated, spontaneous, reversible, stable to electrolytes vs charge-stabilised, made by special methods, coagulated by small amounts of electrolyte |
| Nernst vs zeta potential | Surface to bulk vs shear plane to bulk; zeta controls stability |
| Electrophoresis vs electro-osmosis | Particles move vs liquid moves |
| Coacervation vs coagulation | Two liquid phases vs solid aggregate |
| Peptization vs protective action | Precipitate back to sol vs lyophilic colloid shielding a lyophobic sol |
| Plastic vs pseudoplastic | Yield value vs none; both shear thinning |
| Thixotropy vs rheopexy | Slow recovery after shear vs faster gel formation with gentle shaking |
| Capillary vs rotational viscometer | Single point, Newtonian only vs multipoint, any system |
| Elastic vs plastic deformation | Reversible below yield point vs permanent above it |
| Flocculated vs deflocculated | Fast settling, loose sediment, no cake vs slow settling, compact cake |
| Macro- vs microemulsion | Milky, unstable, needs energy vs clear, stable, spontaneous |
| Creaming vs cracking | Reversible vs irreversible |
| Number vs weight distribution | Microscope/Coulter vs sieve/sedimentation |
| BET vs permeability surface area | Total surface including pores vs external surface |
| Bulk vs true density | Includes voids vs solid only |
| Specific vs general catalysis | H⁺/OH⁻ only vs buffer species too |
| Zero vs first order t½ | Depends on A0 vs independent of A0 |

**Practicals in one line each:** sieve analysis → weight distribution and mean size Σ(% × mean size)/100; microscopy → calibrate eyepiece with stage micrometer, count 300+ particles, dln = Σnd/Σn; bulk density, tapped density, true density (pycnometer) → porosity; angle of repose tan θ = h/r, falls then rises as lubricant increases; Ostwald η1 = η2ρ1t1/ρ2t2; sedimentation volume F = Hu/H0 for different agents and concentrations; Brookfield viscosity at rising and falling rpm → rheogram; methyl acetate hydrolysis k = (2.303/t) log[(V∞ − V0)/(V∞ − Vt)]; ethyl acetate saponification k = (1/at)(Vt − V0)/(V∞ − Vt); accelerated stability → k at 50, 60, 70 °C → log k vs 1/T → t90 at 25 °C.

# Particle size and size distribution by sieving

**Aim:** To determine the particle size distribution and the average particle size of a given powder or granules by sieve analysis.

> Quantities and sieve sizes are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

A weighed sample is shaken through a nest of standard sieves stacked with the largest aperture at the top and the smallest at the bottom, above a receiving pan. Each particle passes down until it meets a sieve whose aperture is too small. The weight retained on each sieve is the weight of particles whose size lies between that sieve's aperture and the aperture of the sieve above. Sieving gives a **weight distribution** and is suitable for particles larger than about 40–50 µm.

The average particle size (weight-based) is calculated as:

**Average size = Σ (% weight retained × mean aperture of the fraction) / 100**

where the mean aperture of a fraction is the average of the aperture it passed and the aperture on which it was retained.

## Requirements

Powder or granules (for example lactose granules, sand, or a granulated blend), set of standard sieves (for example 1000, 710, 500, 355, 250, 180 and 125 µm) with lid and receiving pan, mechanical sieve shaker, balance, brush, butter paper.

## Procedure

1. Clean and dry all sieves; weigh each empty sieve and the pan if weighing by difference.
2. Arrange the sieves in order of decreasing aperture from top to bottom, with the pan at the bottom.
3. Weigh accurately about 100 g of the sample and place it on the top sieve; close with the lid.
4. Shake on the mechanical shaker for a fixed time (for example 10–20 minutes) at a fixed amplitude.
5. Remove each sieve and carefully transfer the material retained to butter paper with a brush; weigh it (or weigh the sieve with its contents and subtract the empty weight).
6. Check that the total of all fractions is close to the weight taken (loss should be small, about 1–2%).
7. Calculate % retained, cumulative % retained, cumulative % undersize and the average size.
8. Plot (a) a frequency histogram of % retained against mean size and (b) cumulative % undersize against aperture size; read the median (50% size) from the cumulative curve.

## Observations and calculations

Weight of sample taken: 100 g

| Passed through (µm) | Retained on (µm) | Mean size d (µm) | Weight retained (g) | % retained | % × d | Cumulative % retained | Cumulative % undersize |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1000 | 710 | 855 | 5 | 5 | 4,275 | 5 | 95 |
| 710 | 500 | 605 | 15 | 15 | 9,075 | 20 | 80 |
| 500 | 355 | 427.5 | 30 | 30 | 12,825 | 50 | 50 |
| 355 | 250 | 302.5 | 28 | 28 | 8,470 | 78 | 22 |
| 250 | 180 | 215 | 15 | 15 | 3,225 | 93 | 7 |
| 180 | 125 | 152.5 | 5 | 5 | 762.5 | 98 | 2 |
| 125 | Pan | 62.5 (taken as half of 125) | 2 | 2 | 125 | 100 | 0 |
| | | | **100** | **100** | **38,757.5** | | |

**Worked calculation.** Average particle size = 38,757.5/100 = **387.6 µm** (weight-average diameter).

From the cumulative undersize curve, 50% of the sample (by weight) is smaller than **355 µm** (median diameter). The modal class (largest fraction) is 355–500 µm.

## Result

1. The particle size distribution of the given sample is shown in the table and the graphs.
2. The average (weight-mean) particle size is ___ µm, and the median diameter is ___ µm.

## Precautions

1. Sieves must be clean, dry and undamaged (no torn or stretched mesh).
2. Do not overload the top sieve; too much powder blinds the apertures.
3. Keep shaking time and amplitude constant between runs.
4. Brush retained material out gently so as not to force particles through the mesh.
5. Avoid sieving very fine or hygroscopic powders that clump; dry the sample if needed.

## Viva questions

1. **What type of distribution does sieving give?** A weight distribution.
2. **What is the lower limit of sieving?** About 40–50 µm; finer powders clump and block the mesh.
3. **What is a sieve number?** A pharmacopoeial designation of a standard sieve, related to the nominal size of its aperture.
4. **Why is the shaking time fixed?** Longer shaking passes more elongated particles and breaks fragile ones (attrition), changing the result.
5. **How is the median read?** From the cumulative % undersize curve at 50%.
6. **Name two disadvantages of sieving.** Unsuitable for fine and cohesive powders; elongated particles may pass end-on; attrition during shaking.
7. **Why should the weight lost be small?** Large loss means particles were lost or stuck in the mesh, so the distribution is not reliable.

# Particle size and size distribution by microscopy

**Aim:** To determine the particle size distribution and mean particle diameters of a given powder by the optical microscopic method.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

Particles spread on a slide are measured against an **eyepiece micrometer**, a glass disc in the eyepiece engraved with an arbitrary scale. Because the value of one eyepiece division depends on the objective in use, the eyepiece scale is first **calibrated** with a **stage micrometer**, a slide engraved with a scale of known size (commonly 1 mm divided into 100 divisions, so 1 stage division = 0.01 mm = 10 µm).

Value of one eyepiece division (ED) = (number of stage divisions × 10 µm) / (number of eyepiece divisions that coincide with them)

Each particle is measured along a fixed direction (Feret's or Martin's diameter), and the number of particles in each size class is counted. This gives a **number distribution** of projected diameters, from which mean diameters are calculated:

dln = Σnd/Σn; dsn = √(Σnd²/Σn); dvn = ∛(Σnd³/Σn); dvs = Σnd³/Σnd²

## Requirements

Compound microscope, eyepiece micrometer, stage micrometer, glass slides and cover slips, sample powder (for example calamine, zinc oxide, starch or sulfur), a liquid in which it is insoluble (for example liquid paraffin or glycerin), dropper, tally counter.

## Procedure

**A. Calibration**

1. Place the eyepiece micrometer in the eyepiece and the stage micrometer on the stage.
2. Focus with the objective to be used (for example 45×).
3. Rotate the eyepiece so the two scales are parallel; make the zero lines coincide.
4. Find a point farther along where a line of the eyepiece scale exactly coincides with a line of the stage scale. Note both readings.
5. Calculate the value of one eyepiece division. Repeat at two or three places and take the mean.

**B. Measurement**

6. Disperse a small amount of powder in a drop of liquid paraffin on a slide; cover with a cover slip, avoiding air bubbles and aggregates.
7. Remove the stage micrometer and focus on the particles.
8. Measure each particle along the eyepiece scale in a fixed direction (do not rotate the slide), and record the size in eyepiece divisions.
9. Move the slide systematically across different fields so no particle is counted twice. Count at least 300 particles (500 is better).
10. Group the readings into size classes, convert to µm, and calculate the mean diameters. Plot a frequency histogram and a cumulative frequency curve.

## Observations and calculations

**Calibration:** 10 stage divisions (100 µm) coincide with 40 eyepiece divisions.
1 ED = 100/40 = **2.5 µm**.

| Size class (ED) | Size class (µm) | Mean d (µm) | Number n | nd | nd² | nd³ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–4 | 0–10 | 5 | 40 | 200 | 1,000 | 5,000 |
| 4–8 | 10–20 | 15 | 120 | 1,800 | 27,000 | 405,000 |
| 8–12 | 20–30 | 25 | 180 | 4,500 | 112,500 | 2,812,500 |
| 12–16 | 30–40 | 35 | 100 | 3,500 | 122,500 | 4,287,500 |
| 16–20 | 40–50 | 45 | 60 | 2,700 | 121,500 | 5,467,500 |
| Total | | | **500** | **12,700** | **384,500** | **12,977,500** |

**Worked calculation.**
- Length–number mean dln = 12,700/500 = **25.4 µm**
- Surface–number mean dsn = √(384,500/500) = √769 = **27.7 µm**
- Volume–number mean dvn = ∛(12,977,500/500) = ∛25,955 = **29.6 µm**
- Volume–surface mean dvs = 12,977,500/384,500 = **33.8 µm**

## Result

1. One eyepiece division = ___ µm with the ___× objective.
2. The size distribution of the powder is shown in the table and graphs; dln = ___ µm, dvs = ___ µm.

## Precautions

1. Calibrate with the same objective used for measurement; recalibrate if the objective is changed.
2. The dispersion must be dilute so particles do not overlap or aggregate.
3. Measure all particles in a fixed direction; do not select particles.
4. Count enough particles (300–500 or more) from many fields.
5. The liquid must not dissolve or swell the powder.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is calibration needed?** The value of one eyepiece division changes with the objective magnification.
2. **What is the size range of optical microscopy?** About 0.2–100 µm.
3. **What type of distribution does microscopy give?** A number distribution of projected diameters.
4. **Define Feret's diameter.** Distance between two parallel tangents on opposite sides of the particle image, drawn in a fixed direction.
5. **Define Martin's diameter.** Length of the line in a fixed direction that divides the particle image into two equal areas.
6. **Why count at least 300 particles?** To get a statistically reliable distribution.
7. **Limitations of the method?** Slow and tiring; measures only two dimensions; operator bias; a small sample may not represent the batch.

# Bulk density, true density and porosity

**Aim:** To determine the bulk density, tapped density and true density of a given powder and to calculate its porosity, bulkiness, Carr's index and Hausner ratio.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Organic liquids such as xylene are flammable and harmful: use them in a fume hood with gloves.

## Principle

- **Bulk density (ρb)** = mass / bulk volume, where bulk volume includes the solid, its pores and the voids between particles. It is found by gently pouring the powder into a graduated cylinder.
- **Tapped density (ρtap)** = mass / volume after tapping to constant volume.
- **True density (ρt)** = mass / volume of the solid alone. It is found by liquid displacement in a specific gravity bottle (pycnometer) using a liquid in which the powder is insoluble and which wets it:

  Mass of liquid displaced = W1 + W − W2, so volume of powder = (W1 + W − W2)/ρL

  **ρt = W × ρL / (W1 + W − W2)**

  where W = mass of powder, W1 = bottle filled with liquid, W2 = bottle with powder and filled with liquid, ρL = density of the liquid.

- **Porosity ε = 1 − ρb/ρt** (× 100 for %); **bulkiness = 1/ρb**.
- **Carr's index = (ρtap − ρb)/ρtap × 100**; **Hausner ratio = ρtap/ρb**.

## Requirements

Powder (for example lactose, calcium carbonate, talc), 100 ml graduated cylinder, tapped density apparatus (or tapping by hand on a pad from a fixed height), specific gravity bottle (25 or 50 ml), a non-solvent liquid of known density (for example xylene, liquid paraffin or kerosene, depending on the powder), balance, funnel, thermometer.

## Procedure

**A. Bulk and tapped density**

1. Weigh accurately about 25 g of the powder (passed through a coarse sieve to break lumps).
2. Pour it gently through a funnel into a dry 100 ml graduated cylinder without compacting. Level the surface without pressing and read the bulk volume.
3. Tap the cylinder from a fixed height (or on the tapping apparatus, for example 500 taps, then another 750) until the volume no longer changes. Read the tapped volume.
4. Repeat three times and take the mean.

**B. True density (liquid displacement)**

5. Clean, dry and weigh the specific gravity bottle (W0).
6. Fill with the liquid, insert the stopper, wipe dry and weigh (W1). Note the temperature; obtain ρL (or determine it from W1 − W0 and the bottle volume).
7. Empty and dry the bottle. Add about 2 g of powder accurately weighed (W).
8. Add the liquid to cover the powder; remove trapped air by gentle swirling (or under vacuum). Fill to the brim, insert the stopper, wipe and weigh (W2).
9. Calculate true density and then porosity and the other indices.

## Observations and calculations

**A. Bulk and tapped density**

| Trial | Weight (g) | Bulk volume (ml) | Tapped volume (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 25 | 40 | 33 |
| 2 | | | |
| 3 | | | |

Bulk density = 25/40 = **0.625 g/ml**; tapped density = 25/33 = **0.758 g/ml**; bulkiness = 1/0.625 = **1.6 ml/g**.

**B. True density**

W = 2.00 g; W1 = 45.20 g; W2 = 46.08 g; ρL = 0.86 g/ml (xylene).
Mass of liquid displaced = 45.20 + 2.00 − 46.08 = 1.12 g.
Volume of powder = 1.12/0.86 = 1.302 ml.
True density = 2.00/1.302 = **1.536 g/ml**.

**C. Derived values**

- Porosity (poured) = 1 − 0.625/1.536 = 0.593 → **59.3%**
- Porosity (tapped) = 1 − 0.758/1.536 = 0.507 → **50.7%**
- Carr's index = (0.758 − 0.625)/0.758 × 100 = **17.5%** (fair flow)
- Hausner ratio = 0.758/0.625 = **1.21** (fair flow)

## Result

1. Bulk density = ___ g/ml; tapped density = ___ g/ml; true density = ___ g/ml.
2. Porosity = ___ %; bulkiness = ___ ml/g; Carr's index = ___ %; Hausner ratio = ___. The powder has ___ flow.

## Precautions

1. Pour the powder gently and do not press or tap while measuring bulk volume.
2. Tap from the same height and count taps for reproducible tapped volume.
3. The liquid for true density must neither dissolve nor swell the powder, and must wet it well.
4. Remove all air bubbles from the powder in the bottle.
5. Keep the temperature constant; liquid density changes with temperature.

## Viva questions

1. **Define porosity.** Fraction of the bulk volume of a powder bed that is void space: ε = 1 − ρb/ρt.
2. **Which density is always the highest?** True density, because it excludes all voids and pores.
3. **Why is helium used in modern pycnometers?** Its small atoms penetrate the finest pores, giving the true solid volume.
4. **What is bulkiness?** The reciprocal of bulk density; it rises as particle size falls.
5. **What does a Carr's index of 10% or less mean?** Excellent flow.
6. **What is granule density and how is it measured?** Density including intra-granular pores but excluding inter-granular voids; mercury displacement.
7. **Why does tapping reduce volume?** Particles rearrange into a closer packing and inter-particle voids decrease.
practicals.title: Bulk density, true density and porosity

# Angle of repose and the influence of a lubricant

**Aim:** To determine the angle of repose of a given powder or granules and to study the effect of different concentrations of a lubricant (magnesium stearate or talc) on it.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

When a powder is allowed to flow freely onto a flat surface, it forms a cone. The **angle of repose (θ)** is the maximum angle between the sloping surface of the cone and the horizontal. It reflects inter-particle friction and cohesion: the more cohesive the powder, the steeper the cone.

**tan θ = h / r**, so θ = tan⁻¹(h/r)

where h = height of the cone and r = radius of its base.

Small amounts of a lubricant or glidant coat the particles, reduce friction between them and improve flow, so θ falls. Beyond an optimum concentration, excess fine lubricant may make the powder cohesive again or fill spaces between particles, so θ may stop falling or rise slightly.

**Interpretation (USP scale):** 25–30° excellent, 31–35° good, 36–40° fair, 41–45° passable, 46–55° poor, higher values very poor.

## Requirements

Powder or granules (for example lactose, a granulated blend or microcrystalline cellulose), magnesium stearate (or talc), funnel fixed on a stand, graph paper or a flat board, ruler or scale, balance, mortar and pestle or polybag for blending, spatula.

## Procedure (fixed funnel method)

1. Fix a funnel on a stand so its tip is at a fixed height (for example 2–3 cm) above a sheet of graph paper on a level surface.
2. Pour the plain powder gently through the funnel until the apex of the cone just touches the funnel tip. Stop pouring.
3. Mark the circumference of the base at several points; measure the diameter in at least three directions and take the mean radius r. The height h is the distance from the paper to the funnel tip.
4. Calculate θ = tan⁻¹(h/r). Repeat three times.
5. Prepare blends of the powder with 0.5%, 1% and 2% w/w magnesium stearate by gentle mixing for a fixed time (over-mixing coats particles excessively).
6. Determine the angle of repose of each blend in the same way.
7. Plot angle of repose against lubricant concentration and identify the optimum.

## Observations and calculations

Base radius kept for comparison (example): r = 4.0 cm.

| Magnesium stearate (% w/w) | h (cm) | r (cm) | tan θ = h/r | θ (degrees) | Flow |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2.6 | 4.0 | 0.650 | 33.0 | Good |
| 0.5 | 2.2 | 4.0 | 0.550 | 28.8 | Excellent |
| 1.0 | 2.0 | 4.0 | 0.500 | 26.6 | Excellent |
| 2.0 | 2.1 | 4.0 | 0.525 | 27.7 | Excellent |

**Worked calculation.** For the plain powder: tan θ = 2.6/4.0 = 0.650; θ = tan⁻¹ 0.650 = **33.0°**. With 1% magnesium stearate: tan θ = 0.500, θ = **26.6°**.

In this example the angle fell from 33.0° to 26.6° as lubricant rose to 1%, then rose slightly at 2%: the optimum is about 1%.

## Result

1. Angle of repose of the plain powder = ___°, indicating ___ flow.
2. The angle of repose decreased with lubricant up to ___% (θ = ___°), beyond which it ___. The optimum concentration of lubricant is ___%.

## Precautions

1. Keep the funnel height and pouring rate constant for all samples.
2. Pour gently; do not tap or disturb the cone.
3. The surface must be level and free from vibration.
4. Blend the lubricant for the same short time each time; prolonged mixing changes its effect.
5. Measure the base diameter in several directions.

## Viva questions

1. **Define angle of repose.** The maximum angle between the surface of a pile of powder and the horizontal plane.
2. **Write the formula.** tan θ = h/r.
3. **What angle indicates excellent flow?** About 25–30°.
4. **Why does a lubricant lower the angle of repose?** It coats the particles and reduces friction between them.
5. **Why may too much lubricant worsen flow?** Excess fine, cohesive lubricant particles stick together and fill voids; magnesium stearate in excess also softens tablets and slows dissolution.
6. **Difference between glidant and lubricant?** A glidant (colloidal silica, talc) improves powder flow; a lubricant (magnesium stearate) reduces friction between the tablet and the die wall; magnesium stearate shows both effects at low levels.
7. **Name two other methods of assessing flow.** Carr's index and Hausner ratio; flow rate through an orifice.
practicals.title: Angle of repose and the influence of a lubricant

# Viscosity of a liquid by Ostwald's viscometer

**Aim:** To determine the viscosity of a given liquid (for example a syrup or a glycerin solution) relative to water using Ostwald's viscometer.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

In a capillary viscometer, a fixed volume of liquid flows through a narrow capillary under its own weight. The flow obeys **Poiseuille's law**:

η = πr⁴tΔP / (8lV)

For the same viscometer, r, l and V are fixed, and the pressure head ΔP is proportional to the density of the liquid. So for a test liquid (1) and a reference liquid of known viscosity (2), usually water:

**η1 = η2 × (ρ1 t1) / (ρ2 t2)**

where t = flow time between the two marks and ρ = density. The method measures at a single rate of shear, so it is suitable only for **Newtonian** liquids.

## Requirements

Ostwald viscometer, thermostatic water bath (25 ± 0.1 °C), stopwatch, specific gravity bottle, pipette, rubber suction bulb, distilled water, test liquid (for example simple syrup diluted, or 30% glycerin), chromic acid or detergent and acetone for cleaning.

## Procedure

1. Clean the viscometer with detergent or chromic acid, rinse with water and then acetone, and dry.
2. Clamp the viscometer vertically in the water bath at 25 °C.
3. Pipette a fixed volume (for example 10 ml) of distilled water into the wider limb.
4. Allow about 10 minutes for temperature equilibrium.
5. Suck the water up the capillary limb above the upper mark A using a bulb.
6. Release and start the stopwatch when the meniscus passes mark A; stop it when it passes the lower mark B. Record t2.
7. Repeat to get three concordant readings (within about 0.2 s).
8. Empty and dry the viscometer (or rinse with the test liquid), add the **same volume** of the test liquid and repeat steps 4–7 to get t1.
9. Determine the densities of water and the test liquid at 25 °C with a specific gravity bottle: ρ = (weight of bottle + liquid − weight of empty bottle)/volume of bottle.
10. Calculate the viscosity of the test liquid.

## Observations and calculations

Temperature: 25 °C; viscosity of water at 25 °C = 0.890 cP; density of water = 0.997 g/ml.

| Liquid | Flow time trial 1 (s) | Trial 2 (s) | Trial 3 (s) | Mean t (s) | Density (g/ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Water | 100.2 | 99.8 | 100.0 | 100.0 | 0.997 |
| Test liquid | 150.1 | 149.8 | 150.1 | 150.0 | 1.10 |

**Worked calculation.**
η1 = 0.890 × (1.10 × 150.0)/(0.997 × 100.0) = 0.890 × 165.0/99.7 = 0.890 × 1.655 = **1.47 cP**

Relative viscosity = 1.47/0.890 = 1.65; kinematic viscosity = 1.47/1.10 = 1.34 cS.

## Result

The viscosity of the given liquid at 25 °C is ___ cP (relative viscosity ___, kinematic viscosity ___ cS).

## Precautions

1. Use the same volume of liquid for both water and the test liquid.
2. Keep the viscometer vertical and at constant temperature; viscosity changes markedly with temperature.
3. The viscometer must be completely clean; dust or grease changes the flow time.
4. Avoid air bubbles in the capillary.
5. Start and stop the watch exactly as the meniscus passes the marks, viewing at eye level.

## Viva questions

1. **State Poiseuille's law.** η = πr⁴tΔP/(8lV); flow of liquid through a capillary.
2. **Why is the same volume used for both liquids?** The pressure head and the volume flowing depend on the volume charged; equal volumes make the comparison valid.
3. **Why is the Ostwald viscometer not used for non-Newtonian liquids?** It works at a single shear rate, while their viscosity depends on shear rate.
4. **What does a capillary viscometer actually measure?** Kinematic viscosity (η/ρ), since flow is driven by the liquid's own weight.
5. **Unit of viscosity?** Poise (dyne s cm⁻²); 1 cP = 1 mPa s.
6. **Effect of temperature on liquid viscosity?** It decreases as temperature rises (η = A e^(Ev/RT)).
7. **Name an improved capillary viscometer.** The Ubbelohde (suspended-level) viscometer, whose result does not depend on the volume charged.
practicals.title: Viscosity of a liquid by Ostwald's viscometer

# Sedimentation volume with different suspending agents

**Aim:** To prepare suspensions of a given insoluble powder with different suspending agents and to compare them by their sedimentation volume.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. The readings below are example values to show the calculation; your values will depend on the materials used.

## Principle

The **sedimentation volume (F)** is the ratio of the ultimate (equilibrium) volume of the sediment, Vu, to the original volume of the suspension, V0. In a uniform measuring cylinder, heights can be used instead of volumes:

**F = Vu / V0 = Hu / H0**

F lies between 0 and 1 (it can exceed 1 for a very loose floc network). The closer F is to 1, the larger and looser the sediment and the better the suspension, because a voluminous sediment does not cake and redisperses easily. F = 1 means no clear liquid separates (flocculation equilibrium).

Suspending agents (natural gums, cellulose derivatives, clays) increase the viscosity of the vehicle (slowing settling by Stokes's law, v = d²(ρs − ρ0)g/18η) and may also adsorb on particles and promote a loose structure, both of which raise F.

## Requirements

Insoluble powder (for example calcium carbonate or zinc oxide, 5% w/v), suspending agents (for example acacia 2%, tragacanth 1%, sodium carboxymethylcellulose 1%, bentonite 2% w/v), distilled water, mortar and pestle, five 50 ml stoppered measuring cylinders, balance, stopwatch or clock, beakers.

## Procedure

1. For each suspension, weigh 2.5 g of the powder (5% w/v in 50 ml).
2. Prepare the suspending agent: triturate the gum or cellulose with a little water (or wet tragacanth and acacia first with a little alcohol or glycerin to avoid lumps); disperse bentonite by sprinkling it on water and allowing it to hydrate.
3. Triturate the powder with the vehicle to a smooth paste, then add more vehicle, transfer to a 50 ml measuring cylinder and make up to 50 ml with water.
4. Prepare a control suspension without any suspending agent.
5. Shake every cylinder the same number of times (for example 10 inversions) and stand them on a level bench, undisturbed. Record the initial height H0 (50 ml).
6. Record the height (volume) of the sediment Hu at intervals: 5, 10, 15, 30 and 60 minutes, then at 1, 2, 3 and 7 days.
7. Calculate F = Hu/H0 at each time. Plot F against time for all suspensions on one graph.
8. At the end, note the number of inversions needed to redisperse each sediment completely.

## Observations and calculations

Initial volume H0 = 50 ml for all.

| Time | Control Hu (ml) | Acacia 2% Hu | Tragacanth 1% Hu | Sodium CMC 1% Hu | Bentonite 2% Hu |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 50 | 50 | 50 | 50 | 50 |
| 30 min | 22 | 36 | 46 | 48 | 49 |
| 1 day | 10 | 18 | 34 | 41 | 46 |
| 7 days (ultimate) | 8 | 14 | 30 | 38 | 44 |

**Worked calculation (7 days).**

| Suspension | Hu (ml) | F = Hu/H0 | Inversions to redisperse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | 8 | 8/50 = 0.16 | Many; partly caked |
| Acacia 2% | 14 | 14/50 = 0.28 | |
| Tragacanth 1% | 30 | 30/50 = 0.60 | |
| Sodium CMC 1% | 38 | 38/50 = 0.76 | |
| Bentonite 2% | 44 | 44/50 = 0.88 | Few |

In this example, the order of effectiveness is bentonite > sodium CMC > tragacanth > acacia > control.

```text
 F ^
 1 |o--o__________________________ bentonite
   | \  \_____________________ sodium CMC
   |  \_____________________ tragacanth
   |   \__________ acacia
   |    \____ control
   +-----------------------------> time
```

## Result

The sedimentation volumes after ___ days are: control ___, acacia ___, tragacanth ___, sodium CMC ___, bentonite ___. The most effective suspending agent under these conditions is ___.

## Precautions

1. Use cylinders of the same size and shape, and the same total volume for all suspensions.
2. Shake all cylinders the same way and keep them undisturbed on a level, vibration-free bench.
3. Read the sediment boundary at eye level.
4. Disperse gums without lumps; incompletely hydrated gums give wrong results.
5. Keep the temperature constant, as viscosity changes with temperature.

## Viva questions

1. **Define sedimentation volume.** F = Vu/V0, the ratio of the ultimate sediment volume to the original suspension volume.
2. **What is the ideal value of F?** 1 (no clear supernatant separates).
3. **Can F exceed 1?** Yes, when the loose floc network occupies more volume than the original suspension.
4. **How do suspending agents act?** They raise vehicle viscosity (slowing settling) and may form a structured, often thixotropic vehicle.
5. **What is degree of flocculation?** β = F/F∞, F of the flocculated suspension over F of the fully deflocculated one.
6. **Why is caking undesirable?** A caked sediment does not redisperse, so the dose is not uniform.
7. **Give two clay suspending agents.** Bentonite and magnesium aluminium silicate (Veegum).
practicals.title: Sedimentation volume with different suspending agents

# Sedimentation volume with different concentrations of one suspending agent

**Aim:** To study the effect of the concentration of a single suspending agent (sodium carboxymethylcellulose) on the sedimentation volume of a suspension and to select a suitable concentration.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. The readings below are example values to show the calculation; your values will depend on the materials used.

## Principle

As the concentration of a suspending agent rises, the viscosity of the vehicle rises. By Stokes's law (v = d²(ρs − ρ0)g/18η), particles settle more slowly. A polymer at adequate concentration also gives a structured (pseudoplastic, often thixotropic) vehicle that holds the particles in a loose network. The sediment therefore occupies a larger volume and the **sedimentation volume F = Hu/H0** rises toward 1.

Above a certain concentration, the gain in F becomes small while the suspension becomes too thick to pour or to redisperse easily. The best concentration balances a high F with good pourability.

## Requirements

Insoluble powder (for example calcium carbonate, 5% w/v), sodium carboxymethylcellulose (sodium CMC), distilled water, mortar and pestle, five 50 ml stoppered measuring cylinders, balance, clock.

## Procedure

1. Prepare 0.25%, 0.5%, 0.75% and 1.0% w/v dispersions of sodium CMC in water: sprinkle the polymer slowly on stirred water and allow it to hydrate fully (or use a stock solution and dilute).
2. For each concentration, triturate 2.5 g of the powder with a little of the polymer solution to a smooth paste; transfer to a 50 ml cylinder and make up to 50 ml with the same solution.
3. Prepare a control with water only.
4. Invert each cylinder the same number of times and leave undisturbed. Record H0 = 50 ml.
5. Read the sediment volume Hu at 15 and 30 minutes, 1, 2 and 24 hours, then daily up to 7 days.
6. Calculate F at each time and plot F against time for each concentration, and the final F against concentration.
7. Note pourability (pours freely, pours slowly, does not pour) and the number of inversions needed to redisperse.

## Observations and calculations

H0 = 50 ml.

| Sodium CMC (% w/v) | Hu after 7 days (ml) | F = Hu/H0 | Pourability | Inversions to redisperse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 (control) | 8 | 0.16 | Free | Many; partly caked |
| 0.25 | 15 | 0.30 | Free | |
| 0.50 | 26 | 0.52 | Free | |
| 0.75 | 33 | 0.66 | Slow but acceptable | |
| 1.00 | 38 | 0.76 | Slow | Few |

**Worked calculation.** For 0.5% sodium CMC: F = 26/50 = **0.52**. For 1.0%: F = 38/50 = **0.76**.

```text
 F (7 days) ^
       0.8  |                         o 1.00%
            |                  o 0.75%
       0.6  |
            |           o 0.50%
       0.4  |
            |     o 0.25%
       0.2  | o control
            +---------------------------------> concentration (% w/v)
```

F rises with concentration, but the rise flattens beyond about 0.75% in this example while pourability gets worse. A concentration near 0.75% gives the best balance here.

## Result

The sedimentation volume increased from ___ (control) to ___ (1.0%) with increasing sodium CMC concentration. The optimum concentration, giving a high F with acceptable pourability, is ___ %.

## Precautions

1. Hydrate the polymer completely; lumps (fish-eyes) give an uneven vehicle.
2. Use identical cylinders, volumes and shaking for all samples.
3. Keep the cylinders undisturbed at constant temperature.
4. Read heights at eye level, at the sediment boundary.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does F increase with polymer concentration?** Higher viscosity slows settling, and the polymer forms a structure that holds particles loosely.
2. **Why not use a very high concentration?** The suspension becomes too viscous to pour, measure and redisperse.
3. **Which law relates settling rate to viscosity?** Stokes's law, v = d²(ρs − ρ0)g/18η.
4. **What type of flow does a sodium CMC solution show?** Pseudoplastic (shear thinning).
5. **Name two other synthetic or semisynthetic suspending agents.** Methylcellulose, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (also carbomers and xanthan gum).
6. **What does F = 0.16 for the control show?** The particles settled into a compact sediment that is likely to cake.
practicals.title: Sedimentation volume with different concentrations of one suspending agent

# Viscosity of a semisolid by Brookfield viscometer

**Aim:** To determine the viscosity of a given semisolid (cream, gel or ointment) at different speeds using a Brookfield viscometer and to identify its type of flow.

> Quantities, spindles and speeds are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual, the instrument's manual and your teacher where they differ. The factors below are example values to show the calculation; always use the factor chart supplied with your instrument.

## Principle

The Brookfield viscometer is a **rotational (multipoint)** viscometer. A spindle immersed in the sample is rotated by a motor through a calibrated spring. The viscous drag of the sample on the spindle twists the spring; the twist (torque) is shown on a dial as a reading from 0 to 100 (or as % torque on a digital model).

**Viscosity (cP) = dial reading × factor**

The factor depends on the spindle and the speed; for a given spindle it is inversely proportional to speed (doubling the speed halves the factor). Digital models display viscosity in cP directly.

Because the speed (and so the rate of shear) can be changed, the instrument can show non-Newtonian behaviour:

- Viscosity constant at all speeds → Newtonian.
- Viscosity falls as speed rises → pseudoplastic or plastic (shear thinning).
- Viscosity rises as speed rises → dilatant.
- Readings on the way down lower than on the way up → **thixotropy** (hysteresis loop when dial reading is plotted against speed).

For stiff semisolids that a cylindrical spindle would only carve a channel through, a **T-bar spindle on a helipath stand** moves slowly downward so it always meets fresh material.

## Requirements

Brookfield viscometer (LV or RV model) with spindle set, helipath stand and T-bar spindles (for stiff samples), sample (for example a cream, a carbomer gel or hydrophilic ointment), 250 ml beaker of standard size, thermometer, water bath (25 °C), spatula.

## Procedure

1. Level the instrument using its spirit level and zero it as per the manual (switch on and allow to stabilise).
2. Fill the beaker with the sample without trapping air, and bring it to 25 °C.
3. Choose a spindle and speed such that the reading falls roughly between 10% and 100% of the scale.
4. Attach the spindle, lower it into the sample up to the immersion groove, avoiding air bubbles under the spindle.
5. Start at the lowest speed (for example 2.5 rpm). Allow the reading to stabilise (for example 30–60 seconds or a set number of revolutions) and note the dial reading.
6. Increase the speed stepwise (5, 10, 20 rpm), recording the reading at each (up-curve).
7. Then decrease the speed stepwise back to 2.5 rpm, recording readings again (down-curve).
8. Calculate viscosity at each speed. Plot (a) viscosity against rpm and (b) dial reading (proportional to shear stress) against rpm for up and down runs.

## Observations and calculations

Sample: cream; spindle: example spindle; temperature 25 °C. Example factors for this spindle: 400 at 2.5 rpm, 200 at 5 rpm, 100 at 10 rpm, 50 at 20 rpm.

| Run | Speed (rpm) | Dial reading | Factor | Viscosity (cP) = reading × factor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Up | 2.5 | 60.0 | 400 | 24,000 |
| Up | 5 | 70.0 | 200 | 14,000 |
| Up | 10 | 82.0 | 100 | 8,200 |
| Up | 20 | 98.0 | 50 | 4,900 |
| Down | 20 | 98.0 | 50 | 4,900 |
| Down | 10 | 70.0 | 100 | 7,000 |
| Down | 5 | 57.5 | 200 | 11,500 |
| Down | 2.5 | 47.5 | 400 | 19,000 |

**Worked calculation.** At 5 rpm on the up-curve: viscosity = 70.0 × 200 = **14,000 cP** (14 Pa s).

**Interpretation.** Viscosity falls from 24,000 to 4,900 cP as speed rises: the cream is **shear thinning** (pseudoplastic or plastic). On the way down, readings at each speed are lower than on the way up (for example 11,500 vs 14,000 cP at 5 rpm), so the down-curve lies below the up-curve: the cream is **thixotropic**.

```text
 dial reading ^
  (∝ stress)  |                     o (20 rpm)
           90 |              o  up
              |        o  .    down
           70 |     o .
              |   .   o      area between curves = hysteresis loop
           50 |  o
              +-------------------------------> speed (rpm)
```

## Result

The viscosity of the given semisolid at 25 °C ranges from ___ cP at ___ rpm to ___ cP at ___ rpm. It shows ___ flow and ___ (is / is not) thixotropic.

## Precautions

1. Level the instrument and keep the sample at constant temperature.
2. Immerse the spindle exactly to the groove; avoid air bubbles under it.
3. Use readings between about 10% and 100% of the scale; change spindle or speed if outside this range.
4. Allow each reading to stabilise for the same time.
5. Clean and dry the spindle immediately after use; handle spindles carefully to avoid bending.

## Viva questions

1. **What type of viscometer is the Brookfield?** A rotational, multipoint viscometer.
2. **How is viscosity calculated from a dial reading?** Viscosity (cP) = dial reading × factor for that spindle and speed.
3. **What does a falling viscosity with rising speed show?** Shear-thinning (pseudoplastic or plastic) flow.
4. **How is thixotropy detected?** Down-curve readings are lower than up-curve readings, giving a hysteresis loop.
5. **Why is a helipath stand used?** So a T-bar spindle cuts fresh material in stiff samples instead of rotating in a channel.
6. **Why not use an Ostwald viscometer for creams?** It works at a single shear rate and cannot handle non-Newtonian or very thick materials.
7. **Why is temperature control important?** Viscosity falls as temperature rises, so readings must be at a fixed temperature.

# Rate constant of a first-order reaction (acid hydrolysis of methyl acetate)

**Aim:** To determine the rate constant of the acid-catalysed hydrolysis of methyl acetate and to show that the reaction follows first-order (pseudo-first-order) kinetics.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. The readings below are example values to show the calculation. Methyl acetate is volatile and flammable: keep flasks stoppered and away from flames.

## Principle

Methyl acetate is hydrolysed by water in the presence of hydrochloric acid, which acts as a catalyst:

CH3COOCH3 + H2O → CH3COOH + CH3OH (H⁺ catalyst)

Water is present in large excess and the HCl concentration does not change, so the rate depends only on the ester concentration: **pseudo-first-order** kinetics.

The progress is followed by titrating samples of the mixture with standard NaOH. The titre includes the constant HCl plus the acetic acid formed:

- V0 = titre at zero time (HCl only)
- Vt = titre at time t
- V∞ = titre at completion (HCl + acetic acid from all the ester)

Then (V∞ − V0) is proportional to the initial ester concentration a, and (V∞ − Vt) to the ester left (a − x), so:

**k = (2.303/t) log [(V∞ − V0)/(V∞ − Vt)]**

A plot of log (V∞ − Vt) against t is a straight line with slope −k/2.303.

## Requirements

Methyl acetate, 0.5 N HCl, 0.2 N NaOH (standardised), phenolphthalein, ice-cold distilled water, 250 ml stoppered conical flask, 5 ml pipettes, burette, conical flasks, stopwatch, thermostatic water bath (25 °C).

## Procedure

1. Place 100 ml of 0.5 N HCl in a stoppered flask and keep it in the water bath at 25 °C for 10 minutes. Keep methyl acetate at the same temperature.
2. Add 4 ml of methyl acetate to the acid, shake well and start the stopwatch (when half the ester has been added).
3. Immediately withdraw 5 ml of the mixture and run it into about 20–25 ml of ice-cold water in a conical flask (cooling and dilution practically stop the reaction). Titrate with 0.2 N NaOH using phenolphthalein. This is V0.
4. Withdraw further 5 ml samples at 10, 20, 30, 45, 60 and 90 minutes; quench and titrate each in the same way (Vt).
5. For V∞, heat about 25 ml of the reaction mixture in a stoppered flask in a water bath at about 60 °C for about an hour (or leave it for 24 hours) to complete the hydrolysis; cool to room temperature and titrate 5 ml.
6. Calculate k for each time and plot log (V∞ − Vt) against t.

## Observations and calculations

V0 = 12.0 ml; V∞ = 24.0 ml; V∞ − V0 = 12.0 ml.

| Time t (min) | Vt (ml) | V∞ − Vt (ml) | (V∞ − V0)/(V∞ − Vt) | log of ratio | k = (2.303/t) × log (min⁻¹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 12.0 | 12.0 | 1.000 | 0 | |
| 10 | 12.6 | 11.4 | 1.053 | 0.0223 | 5.13 × 10⁻³ |
| 20 | 13.1 | 10.9 | 1.101 | 0.0418 | 4.81 × 10⁻³ |
| 30 | 13.7 | 10.3 | 1.165 | 0.0663 | 5.09 × 10⁻³ |
| 45 | 14.4 | 9.6 | 1.250 | 0.0969 | 4.96 × 10⁻³ |
| 60 | 15.1 | 8.9 | 1.348 | 0.1298 | 4.98 × 10⁻³ |
| 90 | 16.3 | 7.7 | 1.558 | 0.1927 | 4.93 × 10⁻³ |

**Worked calculation (t = 45 min).** k = (2.303/45) × log (12.0/9.6) = 0.05118 × 0.0969 = **4.96 × 10⁻³ min⁻¹**.

The values of k are nearly constant (mean **≈ 5.0 × 10⁻³ min⁻¹**), confirming first-order kinetics. Half-life = 0.693/k = 0.693/0.0050 ≈ **139 min**.

```text
 log(V∞ − Vt) ^
              |o
              |  o
              |     o
              |        o           straight line: first order
              |            o       slope = −k/2.303
              |                  o
              +-----------------------> time (min)
```

## Result

The reaction follows first-order kinetics. The rate constant for the acid-catalysed hydrolysis of methyl acetate at ___ °C is ___ min⁻¹, and the half-life is ___ min.

## Precautions

1. Keep the temperature constant throughout; k changes with temperature.
2. Note times exactly; quench each sample immediately in ice-cold water.
3. Titrate quickly and to the same faint pink end point.
4. Keep the reaction flask stoppered to prevent loss of volatile ester.
5. Make sure the reaction is truly complete for V∞.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is this called pseudo-first order?** Two reactants (ester and water) take part, but water is in great excess, so its concentration is constant and the rate depends only on the ester.
2. **What is the role of HCl?** It is a catalyst (specific acid catalysis); it is not consumed.
3. **Why is V0 not zero?** The titre at zero time is due to the HCl catalyst.
4. **Why are samples added to ice-cold water?** Cooling and dilution practically stop the reaction so the titre corresponds to the sampling time.
5. **What are the units of a first-order rate constant?** Time⁻¹ (min⁻¹ here).
6. **Does the half-life depend on initial concentration?** No; t½ = 0.693/k for a first-order reaction.
7. **How is V∞ obtained?** By heating a portion of the mixture to complete the hydrolysis (or leaving it long enough) and titrating.

# Rate constant of a second-order reaction (saponification of ethyl acetate)

**Aim:** To determine the rate constant of the saponification of ethyl acetate by sodium hydroxide (equal initial concentrations) and to show that the reaction is second order.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. The readings below are example values to show the calculation.

## Principle

Ethyl acetate reacts with sodium hydroxide:

CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH → CH3COONa + C2H5OH

The rate depends on the concentrations of both ester and hydroxide, so the reaction is **second order**. When both start at the same concentration a:

**k = (1/at) × x/(a − x)**, or 1/(a − x) − 1/a = kt

where x = amount reacted at time t. A plot of 1/(a − x) against t is a straight line with slope k.

**Following the reaction by back titration.** A sample is run into a known excess of standard HCl, which neutralises the remaining NaOH and stops the reaction. The excess HCl is titrated with standard NaOH. As the reaction proceeds, less NaOH remains, more HCl is left over, so the back-titre Vt rises. In terms of titres:

- V0 = back-titre at zero time; V∞ = back-titre at completion
- (V∞ − V0) ∝ a; (Vt − V0) ∝ x; (V∞ − Vt) ∝ (a − x)

So **k = (1/at) × (Vt − V0)/(V∞ − Vt)**, with a in mol/L.

## Requirements

0.04 M ethyl acetate solution (freshly prepared), 0.04 N NaOH (carbonate free), 0.02 N HCl, 0.02 N NaOH for back titration (standardised), phenolphthalein, two 250 ml stoppered flasks, 10 ml and 20 ml pipettes, burette, conical flasks, stopwatch, water bath (25 °C).

## Procedure

1. Place 50 ml of 0.04 M ethyl acetate and 50 ml of 0.04 N NaOH in separate stoppered flasks in the water bath at 25 °C for 10 minutes.
2. Mix them quickly and start the stopwatch. The concentration of each reactant in the mixture is now a = 0.02 M.
3. Pipette 20 ml of 0.02 N HCl into each of several conical flasks in advance.
4. At 5, 10, 15, 20 and 30 minutes, withdraw 10 ml of the reaction mixture and run it into one of the HCl flasks (note the exact time of half-delivery).
5. Titrate the excess HCl with 0.02 N NaOH using phenolphthalein (Vt).
6. **V0:** titrate a blank prepared by adding 10 ml of a mixture of 5 ml 0.04 N NaOH and 5 ml water (same NaOH content as the reaction mixture at zero time) to 20 ml HCl; or calculate it. In this design V0 = 10.0 ml.
7. **V∞:** warm a portion of the reaction mixture in a stoppered flask at about 50–60 °C for 30 minutes (or leave overnight) so the reaction is complete; cool and titrate 10 ml in the same way. In this design V∞ = 20.0 ml (no NaOH left, so all the HCl is in excess).
8. Calculate k at each time and plot 1/(a − x) against t.

## Observations and calculations

a = 0.02 M; V0 = 10.0 ml; V∞ = 20.0 ml. (a − x) = a × (V∞ − Vt)/(V∞ − V0).

| Time t (min) | Vt (ml) | Vt − V0 (∝ x) | V∞ − Vt (∝ a − x) | k = (1/at)(Vt − V0)/(V∞ − Vt) (M⁻¹ min⁻¹) | 1/(a − x) (M⁻¹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 10.0 | 0 | 10.0 | | 50.0 |
| 5 | 13.3 | 3.3 | 6.7 | 4.93 | 74.6 |
| 10 | 15.0 | 5.0 | 5.0 | 5.00 | 100.0 |
| 15 | 16.0 | 6.0 | 4.0 | 5.00 | 125.0 |
| 20 | 16.7 | 6.7 | 3.3 | 5.08 | 151.5 |
| 30 | 17.5 | 7.5 | 2.5 | 5.00 | 200.0 |

**Worked calculation (t = 10 min).** k = [1/(0.02 × 10)] × 5.0/5.0 = 5 × 1 = **5.0 M⁻¹ min⁻¹**.

The constant k (mean ≈ **5.0 M⁻¹ min⁻¹**) and the straight line of 1/(a − x) against t (slope ≈ 5) confirm second-order kinetics. Half-life = 1/(ka) = 1/(5.0 × 0.02) = **10 min**; at t = 10 min exactly half has reacted (Vt − V0 = V∞ − Vt), as expected.

## Result

The saponification of ethyl acetate by NaOH is second order. The rate constant at ___ °C is ___ M⁻¹ min⁻¹ and the half-life (a = ___ M) is ___ min.

## Precautions

1. Use carbonate-free NaOH and freshly prepared ethyl acetate solution.
2. Bring both solutions to the bath temperature before mixing; keep the temperature constant.
3. Note the time accurately at half-delivery of each sample into the acid.
4. Use the same indicator and end point in every titration.
5. Keep flasks stoppered to prevent loss of ester and absorption of CO2.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is this a second-order reaction?** The rate depends on the concentrations of both ethyl acetate and hydroxide ions.
2. **Units of a second-order rate constant?** Concentration⁻¹ time⁻¹ (M⁻¹ min⁻¹).
3. **How does the half-life depend on concentration?** t½ = 1/(ka); it is inversely proportional to the initial concentration.
4. **Why is the sample run into excess HCl?** The acid neutralises the remaining NaOH and stops the reaction instantly; the excess acid is then measured.
5. **Which plot is linear for a second-order reaction?** 1/(a − x) against t.
6. **What would happen if the concentrations were unequal?** The equation k = [2.303/(t(a − b))] log[b(a − x)/(a(b − x))] is used.
7. **Why use carbonate-free NaOH?** Carbonate reacts differently with the acid and indicator and causes error.

# Accelerated stability study and shelf-life prediction

**Aim:** To carry out an accelerated stability study of a drug solution (for example ascorbic acid solution) at elevated temperatures, and to predict its shelf life at 25 °C using the Arrhenius equation.

> Quantities, temperatures and the assay method are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. The readings below are example values to show the calculation.

## Principle

The rate of chemical degradation rises with temperature according to the **Arrhenius equation**:

log k = log A − Ea/(2.303RT)

Samples are stored at several elevated temperatures. At each temperature the drug remaining is assayed at intervals, the order of reaction is found, and the rate constant k is calculated. A plot of **log k against 1/T** (T in kelvin) is a straight line with slope −Ea/(2.303R). Extrapolating this line to the storage temperature (25 °C, 1/T = 0.003354 K⁻¹) gives k at 25 °C, and the shelf life is:

**t90 = 0.105/k** (first order)

**Assay (example):** ascorbic acid is titrated with standard iodine using starch as indicator (ascorbic acid + I2 → dehydroascorbic acid + 2HI). % drug remaining = (titre at time t / titre at zero time) × 100.

## Requirements

Ascorbic acid (or another suitable drug), distilled water, stoppered glass vials or ampoules, ovens or water baths at 50, 60 and 70 °C, 0.01 N or 0.1 N iodine (standardised), starch indicator, dilute acid (for example metaphosphoric or acetic acid) to stabilise samples before titration, pipettes, burette, conical flasks, graph paper.

## Procedure

1. Prepare a solution of the drug of known strength (for example 1% w/v ascorbic acid) and fill equal volumes into a series of stoppered vials.
2. Assay three vials immediately (zero time) and record the mean titre.
3. Place sets of vials at 50, 60 and 70 °C.
4. At fixed intervals (for example 2, 4, 6 and 8 days), remove vials from each temperature, cool them quickly to room temperature, and assay the remaining drug.
5. Calculate % remaining. Plot log % remaining against time for each temperature; a straight line shows first-order kinetics.
6. Find k at each temperature from the slope (k = −2.303 × slope) or from k = (2.303/t) log (100/% remaining).
7. Plot log k against 1/T, extrapolate to 1/298 K⁻¹, read k at 25 °C and calculate t90. Calculate Ea from the slope.

## Observations and calculations

**% drug remaining**

| Time (days) | 50 °C | 60 °C | 70 °C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 100.0 | 100.0 | 100.0 |
| 2 | 97.4 | 94.2 | 87.6 |
| 4 | 95.0 | 88.7 | 76.7 |
| 6 | 92.5 | 83.5 | 67.2 |
| 8 | 90.2 | 78.7 | 58.9 |

log % remaining against time is linear at each temperature, so degradation is first order.

**Rate constants (from day 8 values; the slope of the full line gives the same within error)**

| T (°C) | T (K) | 1/T (K⁻¹) | k = (2.303/8) log(100/%) (day⁻¹) | log k |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 50 | 323.15 | 0.003095 | 0.2879 × log(100/90.2) = 0.0129 | −1.890 |
| 60 | 333.15 | 0.003002 | 0.2879 × log(100/78.7) = 0.0300 | −1.524 |
| 70 | 343.15 | 0.002914 | 0.2879 × log(100/58.9) = 0.0662 | −1.179 |

**Worked calculation.**

1. Slope of log k vs 1/T = (−1.179 − (−1.890))/(0.002914 − 0.003095) = 0.711/(−0.000181) ≈ **−3,930 K**.
2. Ea = −slope × 2.303 × R = 3,930 × 2.303 × 1.987 ≈ **18,000 cal/mol (18 kcal/mol)**.
3. Extrapolate to 25 °C (1/T = 0.003354): log k25 = −1.890 + (−3,930) × (0.003354 − 0.003095) = −1.890 − 1.018 = −2.908; k25 = **1.24 × 10⁻³ day⁻¹**.
4. Shelf life t90 = 0.105/0.00124 ≈ **85 days** (about 2.8 months) at 25 °C.

```text
 log k ^
  -1.2 |                   o 70 °C
       |             o 60 °C
  -1.9 |       o 50 °C
       |                          extrapolated line
  -2.9 | x 25 °C  <------------------------------
       +----------------------------------------> 1/T (K⁻¹)
        0.00335   0.00310   0.00300   0.00291   (1/T decreases to the right)
```

## Result

1. The degradation of the drug follows ___-order kinetics.
2. Rate constants: ___ day⁻¹ (50 °C), ___ day⁻¹ (60 °C), ___ day⁻¹ (70 °C); Ea ≈ ___ kcal/mol.
3. Predicted rate constant at 25 °C = ___ day⁻¹; predicted shelf life (t90) at 25 °C = ___ days.

## Precautions

1. Fill all vials with equal volumes, close them tightly to avoid evaporation and keep headspace the same.
2. Keep oven or bath temperatures constant (±0.5 °C or better).
3. Cool samples quickly and assay them promptly; stabilise ascorbic acid samples in acid before titration.
4. Use at least three temperatures so the Arrhenius line can be checked.
5. Remember the prediction is valid only if the degradation mechanism is the same at all temperatures; confirm with real-time data.

## Viva questions

1. **What is accelerated stability testing?** Storing a product at elevated temperatures (and humidity) to speed degradation and predict shelf life at normal storage by the Arrhenius equation.
2. **What is plotted in the Arrhenius plot?** log k against 1/T (kelvin).
3. **Define shelf life.** Time for the drug content to fall to 90% of its initial value; t90 = 0.105/k for first order.
4. **What is the ICH accelerated condition?** 40 °C ± 2 °C / 75% RH ± 5% RH for 6 months.
5. **Give two limitations.** Mechanism may change at high temperature; not valid for physical instability (emulsions, suspensions), photolysis, microbial or protein degradation.
6. **What is Q10?** The factor by which the rate constant rises for a 10 °C rise in temperature, roughly 2–4 for drug degradation.
7. **Why is ascorbic acid used as an example?** It degrades (mainly by oxidation) at a measurable rate at moderate temperatures and is easily assayed by iodine titration.
